Valuation notice

Each year, ahead of March 1, your county assessor mails a valuation notice stating the full cash value of your parcel, plus the limited property value if the parcel has one (state law). Sellers should read it early. It shows how the county sees the house well before a tax bill shows up.

The notice goes out in writing, by mail or common carrier. Electronic delivery is allowed when the taxpayer requests it. Afterward the assessor certifies the mailing date to the board of supervisors and to the Department of Revenue.

  • A flood, fire, other act of God or declared emergency can delay mailing. In that case the Department of Revenue director may extend the deadline by as much as thirty days, and the extension covers every property the assessor values.
  • For sixty days after mailing, the assessor may correct a notice if neighborhood or classification data led to a wrong opinion of value. A corrected notice is sent only once the Department has approved the new values.

Keep every notice, even ones that look routine. A saved copy lets you compare this year's figure with last year's and spot a jump before a buyer does.

Questions about how a number was reached are fine to ask. Phone the assessor's office. Someone there can explain the valuation. The roll itself, though, changes only through the formal review process, so a phone call alone will not lower your number.

Due dates and delinquency

Arizona splits the real property bill into two payments. October 1 is the due date for the first half, and March 1 of the next year is the due date for the second. Late status does not begin on the due date, and that gap trips up a lot of sellers.

InstallmentDueDelinquent after
First halfOctober 1November 1 at 5:00 p.m.
Second halfMarch 1May 1 at 5:00 p.m.
Total bill of $100 or lessOctober 1, all at onceDecember 31 at 5:00 p.m.

Should a cutoff land on a weekend or legal holiday, it slides to 5:00 p.m. on the following business day (weekend rule).

Because a bill is payable October 1 but not late until after November 1, a sale can close in October with the first half still owing and not yet delinquent. Ask the title company early what it plans to withhold for the county from your proceeds. Bring your last bill to that conversation so the figures can be matched line by line.

The tax lien and your sale

By statute, each year's tax is a lien on the taxed parcel, and it takes hold on January 1 of the tax year. In effect the house owes that year's tax before the owner sees any bill.

Three events end the lien:

  • Full payment of the tax, penalties, charges and interest.
  • A final vesting of title in a buyer at a tax sale.
  • Issuance of a certificate of removal and abatement.

In priority, the tax lien beats other liens and encumbrances. Only liens held by the state and liens for taxes of other years rank alongside it or ahead. A mortgage lender does not stand first in line the way many owners assume.

If a buyer's title company spots unpaid tax, it will insist that the tax be cleared at closing. Ask the county treasurer for a statement of what you owe today and what is about to come due, and do it before a contract is signed. It's a short call that heads off most closing-table surprises.

If the tax goes unpaid

Collection falls to the county treasurer, who sells the tax lien on delinquent property and, after that, forecloses the owner's right to redeem (enforcement statute). The same section protects the county: a minor, insubstantial error in the process leaves the assessment, the lien, the lien sale and the foreclosure intact.

So an owner shouldn't hope a paperwork slip will undo the debt. The better moves are paying the balance before the lien is sold, or listing the house and letting closing pay it off.

Sale dates, the interest rate and the redemption amount come from other statutes and from each treasurer. Call the treasurer for today's figures on your parcel.

Inherited property and beneficiary deeds

Say a house passes by beneficiary deed under A.R.S. 33-405. The assessor then keeps sending valuation notices to the deceased owner's last address until the beneficiary reports in. That means mailing a certified death certificate for the last surviving owner, along with a new address. The rule is in subsection B of the notice statute, and the law treats the earlier mailing as delivered to the beneficiary.

The practical risk is that a notice sits in an empty house while the sixty-day clock runs from mailing, not from when anyone reads it. Heirs planning a sale should move quickly on three steps:

  • Mail the assessor the death certificate and a working address.
  • Check with the treasurer on whether either half of the present bill has gone delinquent.
  • Hand the parcel number to the title company for its tax search.

We see inherited houses with long-deferred repairs regularly, and the tax status is usually the first item we look at.

Selling as-is with property tax open

Selling for cash won't wipe out a tax lien. What it does is shorten the timeline, so the balance gets settled at closing rather than building through another season. On a house that is behind, the title company sends the county its share from your proceeds and gives you what remains.

A typical sequence for an Arizona owner looks like this:

  1. Find the parcel number on your latest tax bill or in county records.
  2. Get the treasurer's current balance and learn which halves are still open.
  3. Review your valuation notice and decide if you intend to dispute the value.
  4. Describe the home to us: condition, tenants, and any liens you already know about.
  5. Compare our offer against the title company's payoff figures before agreeing.
  6. Close, and let the title company pay the county and any other lienholder from the proceeds.

Because we purchase houses as-is, the roof, the repairs and the clutter can wait. The tax balance is the one item that needs real numbers from the county, and the title company will recheck it before the closing date.

Pull together the newest valuation notice, your latest bill and any treasurer letter before making calls. Armed with those, a buyer prices the deal honestly and the title officer quotes a payoff without guessing; absent paperwork is what usually pushes a closing back.

If you'd rather not carry the house through another installment date, tell us your timeline when you call. A quick sale can land before the next half comes due.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Arizona valuation notice mailed?

Before March 1. A disaster or declared emergency can push that back, though never beyond thirty extra days, and only on the Department of Revenue director's say-so. Expect to see full cash value and any limited value.

When is Arizona property tax delinquent?

November 1 at 5:00 p.m. for the first half and May 1 at 5:00 p.m. for the second. Tiny bills of $100 or less are paid once, on October 1, and turn late after 5:00 p.m. December 31. A cutoff on a weekend or holiday waits until the next business day.

When does the property tax lien attach in Arizona?

It attaches every January 1 for that tax year. Payment, a tax-sale purchaser's final title, or a certificate of removal and abatement ends it. Most other liens rank behind it.

Who sells the tax lien on an Arizona house?

Your county treasurer handles both the lien sale and the later foreclosure of redemption rights. Request a payoff figure from that office before listing.

Do heirs get the valuation notice after the owner dies?

Often they don't. With a beneficiary deed, the assessor writes to the dead owner's old address until the beneficiary supplies a certified death certificate and a new one, and that earlier mailing is treated as received.

Who can claim the exemption

Any adult who lives in Arizona can hold a homestead, married or single. The law asks that you be at least eighteen, live in the state, and actually occupy the property.

Three kinds of homes qualify. The first is your interest in a single compact parcel with a dwelling on it. The second is one condominium or cooperative unit. The third is a mobile home, park model, motor home, travel trailer, fifth wheel, houseboat, manufactured home or similar shelter, together with the land under it.

You get one homestead, and a married couple shares one. The dollar limit counts the equity you or the couple hold, not the price of the house. If spouses who shared a home later divorce, the combined protection for that residence still can't exceed the statutory cap, however the equity is divided.

Do you have to file anything?

No. The protection arises by operation of law, so you don't record a claim or sign a declaration to have it. That surprises owners who know states that demand a filed declaration.

A filing becomes relevant in one case. If you own several properties that could qualify, a creditor may send a demand letter by certified mail, return receipt requested, asking which one is your homestead. You have thirty days from receipt to answer, either by recording a homestead exemption with the recorder in the county where the property sits or by sending the creditor a certified letter, return receipt requested.

Ignore the letter and you can assert the exemption later only by recording a claim with the recorder. If you get one while trying to sell, mark the thirty days on a calendar and consider having a lawyer review your reply.

Debts that can still reach a homestead

The exemption stops forced sale under most judgments and liens, but the statute carves out exceptions. A mortgage or deed of trust leads the list: a lender you agreed to repay can still foreclose.

  • A consensual lien, meaning a mortgage, deed of trust or contract of conveyance.
  • A lien for labor or materials under the mechanics lien statute.
  • A lien for unpaid child support or spousal maintenance, if the arrears became a judgment, a lien exists under the family law statute, or the court ordered a specific security interest.
  • A recorded civil judgment or other involuntary lien, but only for equity above the exemption amount.

A sale that the exemption should have prevented is invalid and passes no interest in the homestead. In a contempt case over unpaid support, a court may also treat the exempt portion as a resource the payer could draw on.

How a judgment creditor forces a sale

A judgment creditor that isn't a mortgage lender can seek a judicial sale only if the debtor's interest is larger than the homestead amount plus every prior consensual lien. The officer conducting the sale can't accept any bid that fails to cover the homestead amount, the prior liens and the allowed sale costs.

When a sufficient bid comes in, the money is divided in a fixed order. The debtor gets the homestead amount first. Prior liens come next, then costs, and anything left is applied to the judgment. If the sale never happens, because the creditor gives up or nobody bids enough, the creditor can't add sale costs or attorney fees to the judgment.

In short, the exemption shields a set slice of equity and leaves the rest exposed to a creditor holding a judgment.

What happens to protection after you sell?

The protection travels with the money. It attaches to your interest in identifiable cash proceeds from a voluntary or forced sale and lasts eighteen months from the sale date, or until you establish a new homestead with the funds, whichever comes first. Cash taken out in a refinance isn't covered.

Two habits follow. Park the proceeds where they stay identifiable, such as a separate account, because only identifiable cash is protected. And remember that the parties may rely on the valuation in the final closing disclosure when deciding how much equity existed on a sale or whether a refinance returned cash.

You can hold only one homestead at a time, so buying a replacement home inside the eighteen months moves the protection to the new property.

When a homestead is treated as abandoned

Three things end a homestead: a recorded declaration, deeding the property away or contracting to convey it, and permanently leaving the home or the state. A temporary absence doesn't, because a claimant can be away up to two years without losing the exemption.

A declaration of abandonment or waiver must be signed and acknowledged by the claimant, and it takes effect only once recorded with the county recorder where the property is located. A recorded mortgage or deed of trust is never affected by the homestead claim.

Estate planners like one detail: moving the home into a trust isn't abandonment when the claimant keeps the power to run and revoke the trust.

What you doResult for the exemption
Record a declaration of abandonmentEnds it from the recording date
Deed or contract to convey the propertyEnds it, except a transfer to a revocable trust you control
Move out for up to two yearsStays in place
Move permanently from the home or stateEnds it
Sell the homeShifts to identifiable proceeds for up to eighteen months
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Arizona houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Is it the same as a property tax break?

No. The homestead exemption in title 33 protects equity from creditors. Property tax exemptions fall under title 42 and lower what the county bills, with their own rules and offices. Exemptions for widows, widowers, owners with disabilities and some veteran owners are filed with the county assessor by affidavit.

Bankruptcy has its own rule. The exemption amount is fixed as of the day the petition is filed. If your equity is at or under the cap that day, the home is fully exempt, and gains in value during the case stay exempt too.

The dollar cap adjusts each January 1 for the consumer price index, rounded up to the nearest $100, so any figure you've seen quoted may have changed. An attorney can give you the current number.

Selling an Arizona house for cash

If your equity sits below the cap, judgment creditors can't touch it, so the homestead rules rarely block a sale. The things worth a closer look are liens that survive the exemption and what happens to the money afterward. A few steps help:

  1. Order a title search early so mortgages, mechanics liens, support liens and recorded judgments are known before you agree on a price.
  2. Ask the escrow officer how each lien will be paid from the proceeds.
  3. If a creditor sent a certified demand letter, track the thirty day response window.
  4. Keep the proceeds in an identifiable account if you want the eighteen month protection.

A cash buyer doesn't wait on a lender, which helps when a lien payoff date is near. This page is general information, so have a lawyer review your specific facts before you sign anything.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Arizona homestead exemption automatic?

Yes. It exists by operation of law, so no recording or written claim is needed unless a creditor demands that you designate which of several properties is your homestead.

How long does homestead protection last on sale proceeds?

Eighteen months after the sale, or until you establish a new homestead with the money, whichever is shorter. Cash from a refinance isn't covered.

Can a mortgage lender foreclose on an Arizona homestead?

Yes. A mortgage or deed of trust is a consensual lien, and the exemption doesn't defeat it.

Can I leave my Arizona home for a while without losing the exemption?

Yes. You can live away for up to two years without abandoning it, but a permanent move from the home or the state ends the exemption.

Does a divorce change the homestead cap?

The cap doesn't double. For a home a couple shared before divorcing, the total exemption for that residence can't exceed the statutory amount for either or both former spouses.

What heirs can owe on an inherited house

Arizona doesn't levy an estate, inheritance or gift tax. Two things can still touch an heir: federal estate tax, which only hits very large estates, and income tax on any gain after a sale. Most families spend more energy on paperwork than on tax. You'll need to know who is allowed to sign, whether a court has to be involved, and how creditors get handled. A statute governs each, and skipping a step can stall a closing.

When federal estate tax applies

The IRS wants an estate tax return only when the gross estate, plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, is larger than the cutoff for the year the person died. Simple estates rarely come close. The cutoffs, year by year:

Died inReturn required above
2022$12,060,000
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

A surviving spouse can inherit the leftover exemption if the estate files a timely return and makes that choice. For the house, the number that matters is fair market value on the date of death. Whatever the owner originally paid is irrelevant. Even without a return, get a written appraisal or similar proof of that value.

Who can sell an inherited house

A deed is only good if signed by someone with legal authority, and right after a death that is rarely the relative who lives closest. Arizona usually points to one of three people: a court-appointed personal representative, a successor holding a recorded affidavit, or a beneficiary named in a recorded beneficiary deed. The way the owner held title tells you which.

Under A.R.S. 14-3715 a personal representative may sell, mortgage or lease the estate's real property, for cash or on credit. They must act reasonably for the people with an interest, and a will or court order can cut the power back. Repairs, insurance, and payment of taxes and administration costs fall under the same grant.

Without an appointment there's no closing. Buyers and escrow officers will hold off, since no one can yet deliver good title.

Can heirs skip probate with an affidavit?

Some estates can. The route is an affidavit of succession for real property under A.R.S. 14-3971, and each of these requirements must be met:

  • At least six months have run since the death. A certified death certificate goes with the affidavit.
  • No one has applied for or received appointment as personal representative.
  • The real property is valued at $300,000 or less once liens and encumbrances are subtracted. The county assessment rolls for the year of death supply the full cash value used.
  • Funeral bills, last illness bills and every unsecured debt are paid off.
  • The signers are the heirs or devisees entitled to the property, and nobody else has a claim to it.
  • Federal estate tax doesn't apply.

The paperwork travels in two steps. The court in the county where the person lived receives the affidavit and issues a certified copy. You then take that copy to the recorder serving the house. Standard filing fees apply unless waived.

The statute also offers a second affidavit for personal property up to $200,000, usable after 30 days. That one suits a vehicle or bank accounts, and it can't move the house.

Beneficiary deeds

If the owner recorded a beneficiary deed, the person named in it receives the house when the owner dies and probate is avoided. A.R.S. 33-405 sets two conditions: the document says it takes effect at the owner's death, and it is signed and filed with the recorder of the county that holds the land, all before the owner passes away.

Heirs should know the following:

  • Whatever mortgages, liens and encumbrances were on the house at death remain on it.
  • Until death, the owner is free to cancel by recording a revocation.
  • Where several beneficiary deeds were recorded, the final one before death wins.
  • A will written afterward doesn't cancel it.
  • With no surviving grantee and no named successor beneficiary, the deed is void.

The beneficiary never had to sign or be informed while the owner lived, so a deed can come as a surprise. Look through the recorder's index early.

How long heirs can wait to open an estate

There's a two-year outer limit after death for starting most Arizona probate cases. A.R.S. 14-3108 bars informal probate or appointment, and formal testacy or appointment proceedings, once more than two years have gone by, subject to listed exceptions.

One exception opens the door to a late case if nothing was filed in court about succession or administration during those two years. In that situation the personal representative may keep estate assets only to the extent needed to confirm title with the rightful successors, and no claims can be presented except administration expenses.

When nobody administers the estate, A.R.S. 14-3901 has heirs and devisees take under the probated will or by intestacy. Administration charges, creditor claims, and allowances for a surviving spouse and dependent children still come first.

Creditor claims and the sale

Debts of the person who died can follow the house to the heirs, so clear them before closing or at it. A.R.S. 14-3803 cuts off claims that existed before death if they aren't presented within two years of death plus any notice period, or sooner for creditors who got actual notice or publication.

Claims that come up at or after death, such as contract claims against the personal representative, must be presented within four months of the date performance is due or the claim arises. For other claims the two-year rule governs the later date. None of this limits enforcement of a mortgage or other lien on estate property, so a lender can still pursue the house.

What the recorder needs at closing

Recording a deed takes a completed affidavit of legal value. Under A.R.S. 11-1133, both sides, or their agents, certify the names and addresses, legal description, sale date, total consideration, financing type and the assessor's parcel number.

The form also asks if the buyer will live in the house or rent it out, and whether buyer and seller are related. A deed without a complete affidavit is refused unless it carries a listed exemption.

When the seller is an estate, bring proof of authority too, such as court letters or the recorded affidavit of succession. Your title company can give you its checklist at the start, which saves a second trip to the recorder.

Common problems with inherited houses

Delays usually trace back to three things: nobody with signing authority, debts left unpaid, and a house left vacant. None of them are tax rules, yet each can hold up a closing.

  • No personal representative has been named, so no one can sign.
  • Heirs in different states must all agree.
  • A mortgage or lien outlives the owner and has to come out of the sale proceeds.
  • Back taxes or repairs built up while the house sat empty.
  • Nobody is sure of the date-of-death value.

A cash buyer can purchase the house as it is, so you skip repairs. The title steps above still have to be completed.

A practical order of work helps. First find out how title was held and whether a beneficiary deed is on record. Next decide whether the estate fits the affidavit route or needs a personal representative. Then collect the death certificate, the date-of-death value and a list of debts, and finally call a title company to confirm what it needs. Doing these in sequence keeps a buyer from walking away over a missing signature.

Frequently asked questions

Does Arizona charge an estate tax or inheritance tax?

No. Arizona repealed its estate tax and has no inheritance or gift tax. Federal estate tax applies only above the filing threshold, which is $15,000,000 for a death in 2026.

Can I sell an inherited Arizona house without probate?

Yes, when title comes through a recorded beneficiary deed, or when the estate qualifies for an affidavit of succession (real property worth $300,000 or less after liens, and six months since the death). In other cases a court-appointed personal representative has to sign.

How long do I have to open probate in Arizona?

The general outer limit is two years from the date of death for most informal and formal proceedings. A.R.S. 14-3108 lists the exceptions.

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes, unless the will or a court order says otherwise. A.R.S. 14-3715 covers sale, mortgage or lease of estate real property for cash or credit.

What does the county recorder require for the sale?

An affidavit of legal value attached to the deed. It states the parties, legal description, date of sale, total consideration and type of financing.

Steps of an Arizona eviction

An Arizona eviction runs from a written notice to a filed complaint, a short summons period, a hearing, a judgment, and finally a writ of restitution carried out by law enforcement. A rent case is measured in days or a few weeks, and each stage has a rule behind it.

StageRule that applies
Notice period endsA nonpayment case can't be filed until after the last day of the five-day notice
Complaint filedSummons issues the day of filing under A.R.S. 33-1377
Return dateNot more than six nor less than three days from the summons date
ServiceAt least two days before the return day
JudgmentPossession, late charges, costs and, at the landlord's option, unpaid rent
Writ of restitutionNot issued until five calendar days after judgment under A.R.S. 12-1178

How service of the summons works

The tenant must receive the summons and complaint in one of two ways: personal service, or posting plus mailing. A constable, sheriff or process server usually handles it, either handing over the papers or posting them somewhere obvious and sending a copy by certified mail.

A.R.S. 33-1377(B) deems the tenant served three days after mailing when personal service was tried, a copy was posted conspicuously on the main entrance within one day of issuance, and the summons went out by certified mail, return receipt requested, the same day.

The complaint must be accompanied by a copy of the lease and related addenda. In a nonpayment case, attach an accounting of charges and payments for the preceding six months as well.

What a tenant can do after being served

A tenant may file a written answer or answer out loud in open court, on the record. If the court sets a trial date, it can order a written answer. Common defenses include:

  • Rent was paid in full and on time, backed by proof of payment.
  • The landlord took rent knowing about the default without a signed writing setting terms, which ties to A.R.S. 33-1371.
  • The tenant made repairs after proper notice using a contractor with a license, and the cost, up to $300 or half the monthly rent, whichever is greater, was subtracted from rent.
  • The tenant lives in subsidized housing with different rent rules.

A trial can be postponed for good cause backed by an affidavit, by no more than three days in a justice court or five days in superior court.

Can a tenant stop the eviction by paying?

Often, but it gets more expensive the further the case goes. Under A.R.S. 33-1368(B), before the landlord files, the tenant restores the rental agreement by tendering all past due rent and a reasonable late fee set out in a written rental agreement.

After filing, the price includes attorney fees and court costs on top of rent and late fees. Once the landlord has a judgment, it's the landlord's call whether to reinstate.

If you're a homeowner planning a sale, this matters. A tenant who pays everything before judgment keeps the lease, and the house stays occupied.

The judgment and the writ of restitution

When the landlord prevails, the court enters judgment for possession, any late charges stated in the rental agreement, costs and, if the landlord chooses, unpaid rent through the rental period. It also grants a writ of restitution. Subsection 33-1377(F) covers this.

The writ waits briefly. Under A.R.S. 12-1178 it can't issue until five calendar days after judgment, and a motion to set aside doesn't suspend or delay it unless a judge finds good cause.

A defendant who was lawfully served with a writ and stays in, or comes back to, the dwelling without the owner's permission commits criminal trespass in the third degree. Once the court rules against the defendant, it must give notice of that rule.

Belongings and utilities after the writ

The day after the writ is executed, the landlord may shut off landlord-provided utilities, and the personal property rules take over. A.R.S. 33-1370 has the landlord store the tenant's belongings for fourteen calendar days after retaking possession, using reasonable care in moving and holding them.

If the tenant makes no reasonable effort to recover them in that time, the landlord may donate or sell them. Sale proceeds go to the tenant's outstanding rent and covered costs, and any excess is mailed to the tenant. The landlord keeps records for twelve months after a sale.

The tenant can get clothing, tools of a trade, and identification or financial documents even before storage costs are paid.

When a tenant leaves without telling the landlord

The statute defines abandonment, and the landlord must follow a notice process before taking the unit back. A tenant has abandoned when absent at least seven days without notice, with rent unpaid for ten days and no sign of occupancy beyond belongings. The other case is an absence of at least five days with rent unpaid for five days and none of the tenant's property in the unit.

The landlord then sends a notice of abandonment by certified mail and posts it on the door for five days. Five days after posting and mailing, the landlord may retake the unit if no personal property remains. A security deposit is then forfeited and applied to rent and reasonable costs.

Security deposits when a rented house is sold

A successor in interest takes on the deposit rules. A.R.S. 33-1321 binds whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends, so a buyer inherits the refund duty.

A deposit can't exceed one and one-half month's rent. Within fourteen days after the tenancy ends and the tenant demands it, excluding weekends and holidays, the landlord must give an itemized list of deductions. A landlord who doesn't comply may owe the tenant twice the amount wrongfully withheld.

Removing unauthorized occupants

Narrow cases get different treatment. A.R.S. 12-1173 counts certain unauthorized occupants of a residence as forcible detainers if they refuse a reasonable request to leave and each of several conditions holds:

  • The person asking is the owner or the owner's authorized agent.
  • The property is a residence or used for residential purposes, and the occupant is there unlawfully.
  • The occupant isn't a current or former tenant, a family member, or someone with a prior agreement to live there.
  • No litigation is pending between the owner and the occupant.

In an action against an unauthorized person, the writ of restitution issues immediately after the court signs a judgment. A tenant at will, or a month-to-month tenant whose tenancy has ended, is a separate category under the same statute.

Selling a rented house during an eviction

A pending eviction adds risk and time, but it doesn't block a sale on its own. A buyer paying cash and buying as-is can take the house subject to the lease or wait for possession, depending on how far the case has moved.

  • A tenant who cures before judgment keeps the lease.
  • The writ can't issue for five calendar days after judgment.
  • Showings need at least two days' notice at reasonable times.
  • Belongings left behind are held fourteen days before disposal.

If you'd rather not manage those steps yourself, a direct sale to a cash buyer can include a move-out date agreed in writing.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an Arizona eviction take?

The summons is returnable three to six days after it issues, and a writ of restitution can't issue until five calendar days after judgment. The total depends on notice, service, any postponement and the sheriff or constable schedule.

Can a tenant stay by paying after the case is filed?

Yes, by paying all past due rent, late fees, attorney fees and court costs before the landlord gets judgment. After judgment, reinstatement is at the landlord's discretion.

How long must a landlord keep tenant belongings?

Fourteen calendar days after retaking possession under A.R.S. 33-1370. After that the landlord may donate or sell them.

Is a tenant who stays after the writ breaking the law?

Yes. A tenant lawfully served with a writ of restitution who remains in or returns to the dwelling without permission commits criminal trespass in the third degree.

Does the new owner take on the security deposit duty?

Yes. A.R.S. 33-1321 binds the holder of the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends.

What makes a quitclaim deed valid

Four things must be true of an Arizona deed: it is written, the person letting go of the property signs it, it is delivered, and an authorized officer takes the acknowledgment. Section 33-401 applies this to any transfer of an estate of inheritance, a freehold, or a term longer than one year. Quitclaim wording earns no discount from those basics.

The signature needs a matching acknowledgment, which is the notary's job and what makes a recorder willing to accept the paper. Should the notary block turn out flawed, state law deems a recorded deed acknowledged as of the day it was recorded. Don't lean on that rescue. Ask the notary to complete each line while the signer is still in the room.

Certain regulated grantees, such as entities under titles 6, 10 or 29, are supposed to put their full name, address and state of organization in the deed. Omitting those details does not void it.

Affidavit of property value

Most deeds travel with a joint buyer and seller affidavit, and the county recorder must refuse any deed lacking a complete one unless an exemption is noted on it (section 11-1133). A quitclaim given for no money is one of the exempt transfers.

When the affidavit is needed, expect questions on these subjects: who the parties are and how to reach them, where the tax bill should go, the legal and street description, the date and total price, the down payment and financing, any personal property worth five percent or more of the price, the assessor's parcel number, how the parties are related, and whether the house will be lived in by the owner or rented out.

An answer is required for every line, even if the answer is "not applicable." One blank can make the whole form incomplete, so proofread before submitting.

Exempt transfers

Some transfers skip the affidavit and fee. Quiet-title quitclaims and no-money quitclaims lead the list in section 11-1134, followed by several others. The ones homeowners meet most are below.

TransferStatute reference

Deed of gift11-1134(A)(7)
Conveyance made under a court order11-1134(A)(5)
Deed that confirms or corrects an earlier recorded deed11-1134(B)(2)
Nominal-consideration residential transfer between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, or siblings11-1134(B)(3)
Transfer from a person to a trustee or from a trustee to a beneficiary, nominal consideration11-1134(B)(8)
Spouses to themselves to create community property with right of survivorship11-1134(B)(10)

Write the exemption you are claiming onto the face of the deed itself. A deed that qualifies but never says so can be bounced just like one with no affidavit.

What the recorder checks on the deed

The recorder starts with how the paper looks. Section 11-480 lists the conditions, and a document that fails one may be sent back at the counter.

  • A caption briefly naming the document, such as "quitclaim deed."
  • A legible original that can be copied.
  • Original signatures, with narrow exceptions the law spells out.
  • For anything dated and executed on or after January 1, 1991: width of eight and one-half inches at most, length of fourteen inches at most, and type no smaller than ten point.

Page one needs a clear two-inch band at the top for the recorder's stamp. Within it, the left three and one-half inches can state who asked for recording and where the document goes afterward. A first page that doesn't comply can be saved with a separate cover sheet that does comply and shows the title. Every edge also gets a half-inch margin, though a miss there bears on notice only and cannot by itself justify rejection.

Recording fees

Without a different fee set elsewhere, Arizona recorders charge $30 for each instrument. Papers recorded at the request of the United States, the state or a political subdivision cost $15 per instrument. Both figures come from section 11-475.

A certified copy costs $1 per page or partial page, and the certificate and seal add $3. Because the filing happens at the recorder in the county of the property, check that office's current charges before you mail anything.

One wrinkle: the exemption statute waives "the affidavit and fee required by this article," which is a different charge from the recorder's fee in 11-475. Ask whether an exempt deed still owes the regular recording fee.

When a quitclaim makes sense before a sale

Use it among people who already agree and need title moved or tidied: removing an ex-spouse, adding a spouse, or funding a family trust. When a stranger is paying for the house, the sale deed does the work and the quitclaim doesn't replace it.

A few questions are worth settling first:

  • Whose names must appear on title on closing day? The title company will say who signs the sale deed.
  • Does a mortgage or a tax balance remain? A transfer within the family leaves both in place.
  • Will any money change hands? Real payment ends the no-money exemption and revives the affidavit.
  • Will the title company insure the later sale? Raise it before the deed is recorded.

Timing matters too. A deed recorded just before a sale gives the title company one more transfer to examine, so leave extra days and tell the buyer about the change at the start.

Getting the house ready to sell

If a quitclaim is one piece of preparing for a sale, call us and explain the situation. We purchase Arizona houses as-is, and the title company produces the list of items to clear before closing.

  1. Settle who will own the house on closing day.
  2. Have the deed drafted and signed in front of a notary who fills out the whole acknowledgment.
  3. Confirm caption, page size and margins, then attach the affidavit or state the exemption on the deed.
  4. Record at the county recorder and pay the quoted fee.
  5. Pass the recorded copy to the title company.

Bring photo ID that matches the name on the deed, since a notary will refuse to act when the names differ. If an owner has died or cannot attend, tell the title company at the start so it can say what extra steps apply.

Repairs can be skipped in a cash sale. Paperwork can't, since a rejected deed may hold up the entire closing.

Frequently asked questions

Is a quitclaim deed exempt from the Arizona affidavit of property value?

When it quiets title or is signed for no monetary consideration, yes. That exemption sits at 11-1134(A)(4) and has to be written on the deed itself when you record.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Arizona?

Thirty dollars per instrument is the default recorder fee in 11-475. Government-requested filings are $15. Certified copies are $1 a page plus $3 for the seal.

Does an Arizona deed need to be notarized?

It needs an acknowledgment before an authorized officer, which in practice means a notary. A recorded deed with a flawed acknowledgment is still deemed properly acknowledged from its recording date.

What size must an Arizona deed be?

Documents executed from January 1, 1991 onward can be no wider than 8.5 inches or longer than 14 inches, in type of at least ten point. Reserve a two-inch strip at the top of page one for the recorder.

Can a quitclaim deed fix a mistake in an earlier deed?

A deed confirming or correcting an earlier recorded deed is exempt under 11-1134(B)(2). Whether quitclaim wording is the right fix for your error is a question for a title company or attorney.

What an Arizona beneficiary deed is

Arizona's name for a transfer on death deed is a beneficiary deed. It hands real property to a named person when the owner dies. Under section 33-405, a deed that names a grantee beneficiary and says expressly that it takes effect at the owner's death passes the interest at that moment, subject to every mortgage, lien and encumbrance the owner created or was subject to in life.

The deed decides who gets the house later. It changes nothing about who owns it now. An owner who signs one can still sell, borrow against or live in the property.

Making the deed valid

The owner must sign it and record it with the county recorder in the county where the house sits, and recording has to happen before death. Subsection E makes pre-death recording a condition of validity, so a signed deed sitting in a drawer accomplishes nothing.

The statute leaves owners plenty of room to shape the gift:

  • Several grantees, who can take as joint tenants with right of survivorship, tenants in common, community property, or another tenancy valid in Arizona.
  • A successor grantee beneficiary, with the triggering condition stated on the deed.
  • A conveyance to the trustee of a trust, even a revocable one.
  • The statutory form, which asks what happens if a beneficiary dies first: the gift is void, or it becomes part of that beneficiary's estate.

If every named grantee dies before the owner, the deed is void unless its terms say otherwise.

Changing your mind or selling

The owner can revoke at any time by recording a revocation before death. No grantee must sign or consent. Under subsection I, a grantee's signature, consent or notice is not required for any purpose while the owner lives.

  • With more than one beneficiary deed recorded for the same property, the last one recorded before death is the one that counts (subsection G).
  • A later will does not revoke a recorded beneficiary deed (subsection J).

Owners who plan to sell soon often skip the revocation and simply close, since the sale conveys the property to the buyer and leaves the beneficiary with nothing to inherit. Still, a recorded deed showing up in a title search can prompt questions, so tell your agent or title officer about it on day one.

A sale during the owner's life is among the conveyances the deed is subject to under subsection A. Whether a title company also wants a recorded revocation first is a question for that company.

Mortgages and tax liens stay

Debts stay put. Whoever inherits through the deed takes the house along with its mortgage, deed of trust, liens and other burdens, all of which were in place at death.

A beneficiary who wants to sell must settle the loan, unpaid property tax and any other lien from the sale money. A delinquent tax lien follows the house to its new owner, so request a payoff figure from the county treasurer early.

Recording costs and the affidavit

The recording fee is $30 per instrument under section 11-475.

Most deeds travel with an affidavit of property value and a separate fee. Section 11-1134(B)(12) exempts a transfer under a beneficiary deed with only nominal actual consideration, and section 11-1133 says the exemption must be noted on the face of the instrument at recording. Without a finished affidavit or an exemption notation, the recorder won't accept the deed.

RequirementRule

Affidavit of property valueExempt for a nominal-consideration beneficiary deed (11-1134(B)(12))
Exemption noteMust appear on the face of the instrument (11-1134(C))
Recorded before deathRequired for validity (33-405(E))

Joint owners and several beneficiaries

Co-ownership changes who controls the result. Where owners hold as joint tenants with right of survivorship or as community property with right of survivorship, a beneficiary deed signed by all surviving owners takes effect at the last survivor's death (subsection D).

If fewer than all owners sign, the deed works only when the last surviving owner is among the signers. If the last survivor never signed, the transfer lapses and the deed is void. A surviving joint tenant or spouse keeps rights that outrank the named beneficiary.

With several beneficiaries, subsection B says each takes separate property rather than community property unless the deed provides otherwise. A house with three beneficiaries can therefore need three signatures at a sale, which affects how quickly a buyer can close. Heirs who live in different cities should arrange notary appointments early.

Married couples should confirm how title is held before anyone signs anything, because the way the property is titled decides whose signature the deed needs.

The statutory form

The form in subsection K is brief. In substance it says the owner conveys the described property to the grantee beneficiary effective on the owner's death. A legal description follows, then a choice about a beneficiary who dies first.

Subsection L supplies a separate revocation form. It identifies the recorded deed by recording date, by docket, book, page or instrument number, and by county. A deed is sufficient if it meets other applicable laws and substantially follows the form, though recorders and title companies still check the acknowledgment and the legal description.

If the owner dies without a beneficiary deed

Small-estate affidavits under section 14-3971 offer another route, but only when the numbers stay under the limits.

Personal property can be claimed by affidavit once 30 days have gone by since the death, provided nobody has been appointed personal representative and the personal property, after liens, stays at or below $200,000.

Real property takes longer. An affidavit of succession cannot be filed until six months after death, and the estate's real property, after liens, must stay at or under $300,000 by full cash value on the assessment rolls. In the affidavit the signers swear that funeral and last-illness bills and all unsecured debts are paid, that they hold the property by intestacy or a valid will, that no one else has a claim and that no federal estate tax is owed. They attach a certified death certificate, and the certified copy goes to the county recorder.

Selling an inherited house for cash

The beneficiary's title comes from the recorded deed, effective at the owner's death. It holds up only if the deed was recorded before death and no later revocation or later deed exists.

Put these questions to a title company or attorney before you list or sign a contract:

  • Is this the final deed on file, and did it reach the recorder before the date of death?
  • Did any named beneficiary die first, and what does the deed say about that case?
  • How much mortgage and unpaid tax is on the house today?
  • Do several beneficiaries need to sign the sale?

A buyer who pays cash for an as-is house can take on repairs, clean-out and a tenant, which is a common situation with inherited property. Gather the recorded deed, the death certificate and your latest tax bill before you call so the title search moves quickly. With several heirs, collect everyone's contact details now. One unreachable signer can hold up a closing for weeks.

Frequently asked questions

What is a transfer on death deed called in Arizona?

A beneficiary deed under section 33-405. It transfers real property to a named grantee beneficiary at the owner's death.

Does the beneficiary have to sign the deed?

No. While the owner is alive, no signature, consent or notice to the grantee beneficiary is needed.

When must the deed be recorded?

Before the owner's death, with the county recorder where the property sits. Recording after death does not make the deed valid.

Can I still sell my house if I recorded a beneficiary deed?

Yes. The deed takes effect only at death, so a living owner can sell, or revoke the deed by recording a revocation. A later will does not cancel it.

Does the beneficiary inherit the mortgage too?

Yes. The house passes subject to the mortgages, liens and encumbrances that existed at the owner's death. If only some joint owners signed, the deed is valid only when the last surviving owner was a signer.

When the lien attaches

A new lien lands on every Arizona parcel at the start of January for that tax year, months ahead of the bill (section 42-17153). It is tied to the land and building, which means it stays with the house through a change of owners.

Whether or not the county has mailed this year's bill, the lien exists. Raise it with your title company at the start of a sale so you both know how this year's portion will be paid at closing.

Lien priority against a mortgage

Where does the tax lien stand among the claims on your house? Near the front. Arizona law ranks it above every other lien and encumbrance except two kinds: liens held by the state and liens for taxes from other years.

That puts first and second mortgages, judgment liens and contractor liens behind it. Some practical consequences:

  • Only three things end the lien: full payment of taxes, penalties, charges and interest; final vesting of title in a buyer at a tax sale; or issuance of a certificate of removal and abatement.
  • A sale of the house leaves the lien intact until it is paid, so the payoff is taken from your proceeds.
  • Each year carries its own lien, so old balances pile up beside the current one.

Due dates and delinquency dates

Your yearly bill arrives as two installments: October 1 for the first and March 1 of the following year for the second (section 42-18052).

Lateness begins after a separate cutoff, always 5:00 p.m. If that cutoff falls on a weekend or legal holiday, the next business day at 5:00 p.m. takes its place.

Interest on late tax

After a bill goes delinquent, interest builds at a simple 16 percent annual rate until the balance is paid. Section 42-18053 treats a partial month as a full one, so a closing on the second of the month costs the same interest as one on the thirtieth. Simple interest does not compound.

The county will not collect interest where its own assessor or treasurer caused the delinquency by mistake. Interest is also skipped for an owner who pays the whole year's tax on or before December 31 of the tax year.

A third escape exists for people who just paid off a loan. If the delinquency happens within a year after a mortgage or deed of trust is satisfied or released, the treasurer, once the board of supervisors approves, may waive the interest and other penalties. The waiver is good once per property.

If taxes stay unpaid

Sooner or later the treasurer auctions the lien in February. You remain the owner at that point. The enforcement statute, section 42-18101, directs this sale and a later foreclosure of the right to redeem.

Preparation follows a strict timeline:

  1. By December 31, the treasurer compiles prior-year delinquent parcels and drafts a notice that each lien will be auctioned publicly (section 42-18106).
  2. Each entry lists the owner, parcel number, delinquent years and the amounts of tax, penalties, interest and charges.
  3. The treasurer's door carries the list for at least two weeks before the sale opens, and a county paper prints it once, two to three weeks before the start (section 42-18109).
  4. Each listed owner is mailed a copy at the last known address (section 42-18108).
  5. Bidding takes place in February (section 42-18112).

One limit on timing: unless advertised within five years of delinquency, a sale for unpaid tax generally can't begin after that point (section 42-18105). A stale mailing address is the easiest way to miss these notices, so update yours with the county.

Who buys the lien

Investors bid, and the lowest interest rate takes the lien. As section 42-18114 puts it, the winner covers the whole delinquent tax, interest, penalties and charges while naming a rate that stays at or under the statutory ceiling. Bid-rate interest begins on the first of the month after purchase.

No deed changes hands, so you still own the home. The practical cost shows up when you want clear title. Redeeming means paying the treasurer the sale amount with interest at the certificate rate, taxes the buyer paid later with interest, and statutory fees the buyer paid, minus the processing fee (section 42-18153).

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Arizona houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Redemption certificate

The treasurer collects $10 for a full redemption made without partial payments. After the right to redeem is established and the money is in, a certificate of redemption is issued, and you may record it at the county recorder (section 42-18154).

Record it before listing. A buyer's title company reads the certificate as proof that the lien sale is behind you. Partial payments carry a $5 fee for the first and the last, but they exist only in a county with a population above three million, so most owners won't see them.

Selling for cash with a delinquent lien

Delinquent tax can slow a conventional sale, yet a cash buyer can close when the offer accounts for it. Back tax, interest and any redemption amount come off your check at the closing table.

  • Request the treasurer's payoff before fixing a closing date. A new month adds a whole month of interest.
  • Learn whether February's auction already sold the lien. If it did, you owe a redemption amount, which is more than back tax alone.
  • Look at earlier years too, because those liens stay alongside the current one.
  • Save every notice. A small procedural slip by the county does not wipe out the lien or the sale, so don't plan around one.

Plan the order of steps. First get the payoff, then compare it with the offer, then give the title company the parcel number so it can search for lien sales and older years. Doing these in order keeps surprises off the closing table and shortens the wait for your proceeds. Ask for the payoff in writing and keep a copy.

If the house needs work or has a tenant, an as-is buyer can build the payoff into the closing statement so you aren't hunting for cash beforehand. Pull together your newest bill, any treasurer notice and the parcel number before calling, and ask the title company for a written payoff.

Frequently asked questions

When does the Arizona tax lien start?

At the beginning of January in the tax year, well before the bill. The lien exists from that first day.

What is the interest rate on late property tax in Arizona?

A simple 16 percent a year from delinquency, with part of a month counted as a full month. None is collected if the whole year's tax is paid by December 31 of the tax year or the delinquency came from a county error.

Does the tax lien come before my mortgage?

Yes. Only state liens and liens for taxes of other years rank with or ahead of it.

How can a delinquent Arizona owner get interest waived?

If the delinquency falls within a year after a mortgage or deed of trust was satisfied or released, the treasurer may waive interest and penalties once the board of supervisors approves. You get this once per property.

Can I sell my Arizona house if the county sold the tax lien?

Yes, since you still hold title. The redemption amount is paid from your proceeds at closing, and the treasurer issues a certificate of redemption you can record.

Who owns the house at the moment of death?

At death, ownership passes to whoever the will names, or to the heirs if there's no will. The transfer remains subject to the estate's debts and to administration. Under Arizona's probate code, a person's separate property and half of the community property go to the devisees or heirs, subject to family allowances, exempt property and creditors' rights.

The surviving spouse's half of community property is a special case. It also stays open to administration until the time to present claims ends, and after that only as far as needed to pay community debts.

The practical upshot: an heir can't list the house the week after a funeral. Someone needs legal authority to sign, either a personal representative or a successor named in a recorded affidavit, so find out which route applies before accepting an offer.

Deadline to open a probate

The general limit is two years from the date of death. An informal probate, an informal appointment, or a formal testacy or appointment proceeding can't be started after that, apart from a short list of exceptions.

One exception is a will contest, which may begin within twelve months of the informal probate or two years from death, whichever is later. A late proceeding can also go forward if no court proceeding about the estate occurred in those two years. Then the personal representative may hold estate assets only as needed to confirm title with the rightful successors, and creditor claims other than administration expenses can't be presented.

A missed deadline doesn't always close the door, but it narrows what the representative can do. If you inherited a house long ago and never opened an estate, ask a probate attorney about timing.

Who can ask the court to open an informal probate?

The statute names the people who may apply, so not everyone can. The application goes to the registrar and must be verified. Eligible applicants:

  • The surviving spouse.
  • An adult child, a parent, a brother or a sister.
  • Any heir of the decedent.
  • A person nominated as personal representative in the will.
  • The state veteran services department, if the decedent served.
  • Any creditor, beginning forty five days after death.
  • The public fiduciary, if no one else is qualified and willing.

The application must name the decedent, give the date of death and county of domicile, identify the spouse, children, heirs and devisees, and state that the time limit hasn't expired. When there's a will, the original must be with the court or come with the application, and the applicant must say it appears validly signed and not revoked.

Priority to serve as personal representative

The statute sets the order, beginning with whoever the will names. With no will, or if the nominee declines, it works down a ranked list.

RankPerson with priority
1Person named in the will, including one named under a will's power to nominate
2Surviving spouse who is also a devisee
3Other devisees
4Surviving spouse
5Other heirs
6State veteran services department, for a veteran or a veteran's spouse or child
7A creditor, after forty five days
8Public fiduciary

Objections to an appointment can be raised only in a formal proceeding. A formal proceeding is also required when someone with higher priority hasn't renounced, when people sharing a priority haven't agreed, or when someone without priority seeks appointment. A minor, a foreign corporation, or anyone the court finds unsuitable can't serve.

What the personal representative must do after appointment

Two jobs come first: inventory the estate and warn creditors. Within ninety days of appointment the representative prepares an inventory showing what the decedent owned, the value on the date of death, whether each item was community or separate property, and any encumbrance. It may be filed with the court or mailed to the heirs or devisees and to anyone who asks.

Creditors hear about the death in two ways. The representative publishes a notice once a week for three straight weeks in a county newspaper and mails written notice to known creditors. A creditor generally has four months after first publication, or sixty days after receiving mailed notice if that's later, to present a claim.

The claim period has an outer cap even without notice. Claims that arose before death are barred two years after death, plus any time left in a notice period that was started.

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes. A personal representative acting reasonably for the interested persons may acquire or dispose of an asset, Arizona land included, for cash or on credit and at public or private sale. The representative can also sell, mortgage or lease estate real property, unless the will or a court order restricts it.

Supervised administration changes things. There, every sale of real property needs court confirmation, and no distribution can be made without a prior court order. Buyers and title companies will want to see letters proving the representative's authority and whether the estate is supervised.

After a sale, or when the house passes to an heir in kind, the representative signs a deed of distribution. A deed of distribution recorded with a county recorder must list the name and address of each distributee.

Skipping full probate on a smaller estate

Arizona offers affidavits for small estates when no personal representative has been appointed or is pending. Successors can collect personal property by affidavit thirty days after death if it totals $200,000 or less after liens. For Arizona real property, a successor affidavit is allowed six months after death when the property, after liens, has a full cash value of no more than $300,000 at death.

The real property affidavit has added conditions. Debts and funeral expenses must be paid, nobody else may claim the property, and no federal estate tax can be due. You attach a certified death certificate and file with the superior court in the county of domicile, and the registrar's certified copy is recorded with the county recorder.

Someone who buys from a successor named in the recorded copy gets the same protection as a buyer from a distributee under a personal representative's deed of distribution.

Intestate shares for a surviving spouse

Without a will, the surviving spouse takes the whole intestate estate if the decedent left no children, or only children who are also the spouse's. When any child isn't the spouse's, the spouse takes half of the intestate separate property and nothing from the decedent's half of community property.

In a blended family, that can leave a house shared between a surviving spouse and children from another relationship. Ask early who must sign the deed.

What heirs should gather before selling

Begin with papers that prove who can sign. Having them ready lets you answer a buyer's questions fast.

  • A certified death certificate.
  • The original will, if one exists, and the court's order or letters of appointment.
  • The deed or title report and payoff statements for any mortgage.
  • Property tax bills, since half is due October 1 and half March 1.
  • A list of heirs with current mailing addresses, for the deed of distribution.

Next, line up the sequence: authority first, then a title review, then a price. A cash buyer can close on the house as-is, which spares heirs from repairs while they handle the court steps. Frequently asked questions

How long do you have to start probate in Arizona?

Generally two years from the date of death. Exceptions include a will contest and a case where no court proceeding about the estate occurred in those two years.

How long does a creditor have to file a claim against an estate?

Usually four months after the first newspaper notice, or sixty days after mailed notice if later. Claims are also barred two years after death, subject to the statute.

Does a personal representative need court approval to sell the house?

Not in an unsupervised estate, where the representative may sell at public or private sale. In a supervised administration, every sale of real property needs court confirmation.

Can heirs sell an Arizona house without probate?

Possibly. A successor affidavit for real property is available six months after death when the property is worth $300,000 or less after liens and other conditions are met, and the certified copy is recorded with the county recorder.

When must the personal representative prepare an inventory?

Within ninety days after appointment. It lists the decedent's property, its date-of-death value, whether it was community or separate and any encumbrance.

How Arizona taxes the gain on a house

Arizona has no separate capital gains tax. A profit from selling a house flows into your individual income tax return, and the state taxes the entire taxable income of residents and the Arizona-source income of nonresidents under A.R.S. 43-1011. A house is a capital asset, so the gain counts as income unless a rule removes it.

The one gain-specific break is a subtraction in paragraph 22 of A.R.S. 43-1022. It removes a share of net long-term capital gain that is included in your federal adjusted gross income.

Two questions decide what you owe on a house sale: how much gain the federal home sale exclusion wipes out, and whether what's left qualifies for the Arizona subtraction. For the income tax rate on your return, ask the Arizona Department of Revenue or a tax professional.

The 25 percent Arizona subtraction

For tax years beginning after December 31, 2014, you can subtract 25 percent of net long-term capital gain, but only on assets acquired after December 31, 2011. The break started smaller and was phased up: ten percent for the first covered year, twenty percent the next, then twenty-five percent from 2014 forward.

The test looks at when you acquired the asset, so a house bought before 2012 doesn't qualify. If you can't prove the acquisition date, the subtraction is denied. Hold on to the closing statement from your purchase.

The subtraction also reaches only long-term gain. A house held one year or less produces short-term gain, so a quick flip gets no Arizona subtraction.

The federal home sale exclusion

The first thing that shrinks your taxable gain is the federal exclusion for a main home: $250,000 for a single filer, $500,000 on a joint return. Gain that's excluded never lands in federal adjusted gross income, and since Arizona's subtraction only works on gain that does land there, the exclusion goes first and the state break applies to the remainder.

Four conditions decide whether you get it:

  • You owned the home for at least 24 months during the 5 years ending on the sale date.
  • You lived there as your residence for at least 24 months within that same 5-year window. The two 24-month stretches can fall in different years.
  • On a joint return, one spouse can satisfy the ownership condition, but both spouses must satisfy the residence condition.
  • You generally can't have claimed the exclusion on a different home in the two years before this sale.

A rental property or a house you never lived in will usually miss the residence condition, which can leave the full gain taxable.

Reporting the sale

An excluded gain can still need a line on your return. Should you get a Form 1099-S, report the sale even if every dollar of gain is excludable. You also report it when part of the gain can't be excluded.

The mechanics run through Form 8949 and Schedule D with your Form 1040. IRS Publication 523, Selling Your Home, includes worksheets. Selling on an installment plan doesn't cost you the exclusion, even if some of the price comes in a later year.

Long-term versus short-term gain

Ownership of more than a year makes the gain long-term. Owning a year or less makes it short-term and taxes it like wages. Count from the day after you acquired the house up to and including the day of sale.

Federal long-term rates start at zero. For 2025 tax years, these taxable income ceilings mark where the zero rate on net capital gain stops:

How you fileZero rate applies up to taxable income of
Single or married filing separately$48,350
Married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse$96,700
Head of household$64,750

Above those levels, most individuals pay 15 percent on most net capital gain, and 20 percent applies at the top bracket. Depreciation taken on a rental house creates unrecaptured section 1250 gain, and that slice is taxed at a maximum of 25 percent.

Inherited or gifted houses

For the Arizona subtraction, someone who inherits a house or receives it as a gift is treated as having acquired it on the date the previous owner did. So a house your parent bought in 2005 fails the post-2011 acquisition test even if you inherited it last year, while one bought in 2015 passes.

Your federal basis in an inherited or gifted house isn't what you paid, and IRS Publication 551 covers that rule. Basis drives the size of the gain, so get the date-of-death value documented, for example with an appraisal, before you list or sign a sale contract.

Capital losses on a house

If you sell your personal residence for less than you paid, you can't deduct the loss. The same goes for a personal car.

An investment house is different. Arizona gives a subtraction when a capital loss carryover under A.R.S. 43-1029 is larger than the federal carryover, so losses carried from earlier years may help on a later gain. Federally, net capital losses offset other income up to $3,000 a year, or $1,500 for married filing separately, and the unused balance carries forward.

Recording the deed and the affidavit of legal value

Before a county recorder in Arizona will accept your deed, the sale details must be sworn. A.R.S. 11-1133 requires an affidavit of legal value with each deed and any sale contract, signed by the buyer and seller or an agent. Expect to supply:

  • Names and mailing addresses for both sides
  • Legal description, situs address and assessor's parcel number
  • Sale date and the total consideration paid
  • The financing type: cash, a new third-party loan, seller financing, an assumption or an exchange
  • Whether the house will be lived in by the owner or rented out

A recorder has to turn away any deed that lacks a complete affidavit, unless a listed exemption applies. That sale price is also the number you'll use for your gain, so check it against the settlement statement.

Records to keep for your tax return

Basis starts with what you paid. Improvements that add value push it up, while allowable depreciation and insurance payments for casualty losses pull it down. That's why the paper trail matters. Keep:

  • The closing statement from your purchase, which doubles as proof of the acquisition date for the 25 percent subtraction
  • Invoices for additions, a roof, an HVAC system and similar capital work
  • The 1099-S or final settlement statement showing gross proceeds
  • A record of the days you lived in the home, so you can show you met the ownership and use tests
  • Worksheets for any capital loss carried over from a prior year

Selling as-is doesn't change the rule: only improvements you paid for raise basis. Hand these papers to your tax preparer, ideally before you list the house.

Frequently asked questions

Does Arizona have its own capital gains tax rate?

No. The gain on a house is taxed as part of your individual income, with a subtraction of 25 percent of net long-term capital gain for assets acquired after December 31, 2011. Ask the Arizona Department of Revenue or a tax professional for the rate that applies to your return.

Can I use the 25 percent subtraction on a house I bought in 2008?

No. A.R.S. 43-1022 covers only gain from assets acquired after December 31, 2011, so a 2008 purchase doesn't qualify.

What if I can't prove when my parent bought the house I inherited?

The subtraction is denied. If the acquisition date can't be verified, no subtraction is allowed, and for an inherited house the date that counts is the one on which the person who died acquired it.

Do I owe tax if I lived in the house for two years?

You may owe nothing federally on gain up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you meet the ownership and use tests. Gain above those limits is still reported and may be taxed, and you must report the sale if you receive a 1099-S.

Is a loss on my house deductible in Arizona?

No. Losses on the sale of personal-use property such as a home aren't deductible.

How an Arizona tax sale works

Don't picture a courthouse-steps house auction. Arizona sells a lien first and a deed only later, and only if nobody redeems. Each February the county treasurer auctions liens on delinquent real property to the public, and the winning bidder gets a certificate of purchase, not the house.

You keep title, you keep living there and you keep the right to sell. All the sale does is put an investor in line to earn interest and, down the road, to sue for the property if the lien is never redeemed. The design gives an owner more time than most people assume, but the clock is running.

Stages from delinquency to a possible deed

Four stages separate a missed payment from a possible deed. Each rests on its own statute, and each is a moment when you can step in.

StageWhat happensStatute
DelinquencyTaxes unpaid after the November 1 or May 1 cutoff at 5:00 p.m.42-18052
Lien saleTreasurer sells the lien at auction in February42-18112
Redemption windowOwner or others may redeem any time within three years, and after that until a treasurer's deed is delivered42-18152
Foreclosure suitLien holder sues in superior court to foreclose the right to redeem42-18201

The first three stages can stretch across years before a suit is even possible, so a delinquent parcel may look quiet while interest keeps building.

Bidding at the lien auction

Bidders compete to take the lowest interest rate. The winner pays the entire delinquent amount, and section 42-18114 caps the rate at the limit computed under section 42-18053. Interest at the bid rate starts on the first day of the month following the purchase.

That is the reverse of an ordinary auction, because the lower rate wins. The treasurer keeps the sale going day by day, skipping Sundays and holidays, until every parcel has been offered and bids dry up (section 42-18112).

How long you have to redeem

You may redeem for three years from the sale date, and afterward until the treasurer delivers a deed. Both periods appear in section 42-18152.

The price of redemption has three parts, laid out in section 42-18153:

  • What the lien sold for, plus interest at the certificate of purchase rate.
  • Taxes that came due after the sale and were paid by the purchaser, with interest at the same rate.
  • Statutory fees the purchaser paid on the certificate, leaving out the processing fee.

Pay the treasurer, and a certificate of redemption follows. The holder may record it with the county recorder.

When the lien buyer can sue

Not until three years after the sale, and not later than ten years from the end of the month the lien was acquired. Section 42-18201 lets the purchaser, or the state when it holds the lien, bring an action to foreclose the right to redeem.

The case is filed in superior court in the property's county, with the county treasurer named as a party. Should a law or court order bar filing, the deadline extends twelve months past the end of that bar.

If you are served, call an attorney or the treasurer the same week and ask for the exact redemption figure. Figures change as interest accrues, so request an updated one before you send payment.

Here an owner can no longer afford to wait. Read any papers the day they are served. Redemption stays available until a judgment ends the right, and paying the redemption amount before then stops the case.

Excess proceeds sale

If the house is worth far more than the lien, the court can order a sale so the owner's equity isn't lost. Under section 42-18204, a sale counts as reasonable when the likely price is more than $2,500 above the total owed to the lien holder.

Either side may request the finding. The lien holder reports its costs, the lien amount with 16 percent interest from the sale date, and fees. The owner offers a reasonable estimate of market value. On a grant, the court orders a sale and sets an opening bid, and the owner's claim to the excess survives.

When the court finds no reasonable excess sale, it enters judgment foreclosing the right to redeem and directs the treasurer to deliver a deed to the winning party. After that, subject to appeal, the former owner holds no right, title or interest. Easements and certain assessment liens survive.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Arizona houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Notice before the sale

The treasurer mails a notice of the proposed sale to the owner at the last known address (section 42-18108). An outdated address is a real risk with inherited homes and rentals, since the notice can reach a mailbox no one checks.

Notice also goes public. The list is posted at the treasurer's door for at least two weeks before bidding starts and printed once in a county newspaper two to three weeks before the start date. If the treasurer misses a minor step, the statute treats an insubstantial failure to comply as no ground to invalidate the sale.

Timeline from start to finish

The statutes set a floor and a ceiling, and the space between them is wide. No foreclosure suit can come sooner than three years after the lien sale.

Start at delinquency. A sale for unpaid tax must begin within five years of that point unless it was advertised within the period (section 42-18105). The auction itself happens in February. Then the three-year mark opens the door to a suit, and ten years after the month the lien was acquired closes it, with twelve more months if a law or order blocks filing (section 42-18201).

Treat the three-year mark as a planning deadline even though redemption remains possible after it.

Selling before or after the tax sale

You can sell at either point, because you keep title until a deed is delivered. Before the February auction, the delinquent tax and interest come out of your proceeds. After the lien sale, the redemption amount comes out instead.

  • Get the treasurer's payoff in writing and check older tax years, since liens for other years survive.
  • Ask whether a certificate of purchase exists and who holds it.
  • Confirm that no foreclosure action is pending in superior court.
  • Expect the deed to carry an exemption note or an affidavit of property value, and a recording fee of $30 per instrument under section 11-475.

A buyer paying cash and taking the house as-is can often close faster than one relying on a loan, because there is no lender appraisal to wait for.

Frequently asked questions

Does Arizona sell the house at a tax sale?

Not at first. The county sells the tax lien and you keep the house. A deed follows only if the lien holder wins a foreclosure of the right to redeem.

How long do I have to redeem an Arizona tax lien?

Three years after the lien sale, and then until the treasurer delivers a deed to the certificate holder. You pay the county treasurer.

Can an investor sue right away after buying the lien?

No. Foreclosure can start no sooner than three years after the sale and must be filed within ten years after the month the lien was acquired.

What happens if my house is worth much more than the tax debt?

Either side can ask the court for an excess proceeds sale. It is treated as reasonable when the likely price is more than $2,500 above what the lien holder is owed, and your interest in the excess survives.

Where do I record a certificate of redemption?

At the county recorder's office in the county where the property sits. Recording is optional but shows a title company the lien was cleared.
