What to bring to the recorder

A deed clears the counter when you present a signed, notarized original, a finished affidavit of property value (or a stated exemption), and the recording fee. The deed rules come from section 33-401 and the affidavit rules from section 11-1133, and the county recorder applies both on presentation.

Go down this list before heading out:

  • The original deed, with original ink signatures. Photocopies don't satisfy the original-document rule.
  • A notary acknowledgment completed by an officer Arizona law authorizes.
  • A caption near the top naming the document, for example "warranty deed" or "special warranty deed."
  • The assessor's parcel number and the full legal description.
  • The address where the tax bill should be sent.
  • The affidavit of property value signed by both parties or their agents, or a clear exemption notation.
  • A check or other payment the county recorder accepts.

Where deeds are recorded and who files them

Filing is done by the county recorder. When a house sells, the title or escrow agent usually takes the deed over once funds are in. The fee statute, section 11-475, is built around that office, and the affidavit statute points to the same officer.

Cash sales follow a set sequence. The buyer's money is deposited, the title company confirms payoff figures, the deed is signed, and only then does the document go to the recorder. Some sellers think the sale is final at the signing table. The public record changes only after the recorder accepts the deed.

Use the recorder in the county where the house sits. An owner who lives in a different county still deals with the property's county.

Recording fees and certified copies

Recorders default to $30 per instrument. Certified copies add up page by page, plus a seal charge. The full schedule from section 11-475 is below.

ServiceFee
Recording papers with no other fee specified$30 per instrument
Papers recorded at the request of the United States, the state or a political subdivision$15 per instrument
Certified copy of a record$1 per page or partial page
Recorder's certificate and seal on a copy$3 added
Certificate under section 47-9523$10 per name, plus $1 per financing statement

State agencies requesting copies for official use pay half the copy fee. A recorder also can't bill a county office for recording a document where public money would cover the charge.

Formatting problems that get a deed rejected

A recorder may reject an instrument that has no caption, isn't an original, is hard to read, lacks original signatures or exceeds the size limits. section 11-480 lists those grounds, and they are the only ones the counter may use to refuse a document on form.

  • Documents executed on or after January 1, 1991 can't be wider than 8.5 inches or longer than 14 inches.
  • Type must be ten point or larger.
  • Every edge gets a half-inch margin. Text inside it may not count as notice unless the recorder's copy reproduces it, but that alone is not a reason to reject.
  • Page one needs a top margin of at least two inches, kept clear for the recording stamp.

A document that changes an earlier recorded one must state the earlier recording date plus the docket and page. After the recorder accepts a document, the statute bars later attacks based on these form rules.

Affidavit of property value and exemptions

The affidavit is a shared form, signed by both sides, that reports the price, the financing and who the parties are. The recorder must refuse a deed without it unless an exemption is noted. section 11-1133 requires it for each deed that transfers title and each contract for sale of real property.

Expect further questions: was personal property included in the price, what kind of financing was used (cash, new third-party loan, seller loan, assumed loan or exchange), and will the buyer move in or rent it out. A separate declaration, due within four months, applies to beneficiaries of a foreclosed trustee's deed who receive extra insurance money.

The exemptions are in section 11-1134. They include deeds of gift, court-ordered conveyances, sales for delinquent taxes, partitions, moves into or out of a joint tenancy, and transfers caused by a legal name change. Mark the specific exemption you claim on the face of the deed. A general note that the transfer is exempt won't satisfy the statute.

Notary errors after recording

Once the deed is recorded, a flaw in the notary block does not sink it. Under section 33-401(D), a defect, omission or informality in the acknowledgment, or a lapse in how it was taken, leaves a recorded deed treated as duly acknowledged from its recording date.

That protects the past. It is no reason to be casual now. Ask your title company whether it wants a corrected deed before closing, and if you catch a mistake before recording, fix it first.

Step by step on closing day

Few sellers ever walk into the recorder's office. Behind the scenes, a sale typically unfolds like this.

  1. At the title company, you sign and a notary finishes the acknowledgment.
  2. Buyer funds arrive, and loans, tax balances and other liens get paid off.
  3. Escrow staff add the affidavit or the exemption notation and send everything to the recorder.
  4. The recorder checks form, caption, signatures and fee. A problem here sends the package back.
  5. On acceptance the deed joins the public record, and you collect your net proceeds.

If you handle recording yourself, for instance on a transfer between relatives, phone the recorder beforehand to learn what payment it takes and whether walk-in filings are accepted. Small procedural differences between counties are common. Keep the recording receipt with your closing papers.

How recording fits a fast sale

Think of recording as the finish line. A deed problem pushes back the day the buyer's name shows in the public record, which is why we ask for your vesting deed early and why the title company reads it before closing.

For a quick sale, these four items decide how smoothly recording goes:

  1. The name on the deed matches the name on the seller's ID.
  2. Any deceased owner has been handled through the proper estate or deed steps.
  3. Liens, tax balances and loans have payoff figures.
  4. The affidavit of property value is filled in or an exemption is marked.

We buy houses as-is across Arizona. Send the address and what you know about title, and we'll tell you plainly what the title company is likely to ask for. After closing, the recorder's stamped copy shows the new owner's name, and a certified copy is available for the fee above.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Arizona?

At the recorder's office in the county where the property sits. In a sale, the title or escrow company usually submits the deed once the buyer's funds arrive.

What is the Arizona deed recording fee?

It is $30 per instrument under section 11-475 when no other fee is stated. Recordings requested by a government body run $15 per instrument.

What can cause an Arizona recorder to reject a deed?

A missing caption, a copy instead of an original, an illegible page, missing original signatures, or a page over 8.5 inches wide or 14 inches long, or type under ten point. A missing affidavit with no exemption notation is another reason.

Do I need a notary to record a deed in Arizona?

Yes. The grantor signs and acknowledges before an authorized officer. If the acknowledgment is later found defective, a recorded deed is still treated as properly acknowledged from its recording date.

How much is a certified copy of a recorded deed?

$1 for each page or partial page, plus $3 for the recorder's certificate and seal.
